transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, uh… I guess it’s the eating. Mostly after late shifts. I’ll get off work and tell myself I’m just grabbing something quick, you know, like takeout on the way home, and then it turns into two burgers, fries, a shake… and then I still go home and pick through leftovers in the garage like it’s a whole second supper.

It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud. I work production, so late shifts kind of mess with your head anyway, and there’s this burger place that stays open late near the plant—anyway, that’s… that’s why I’m here.
Do you feel guilty after these late-night eating episodes?

Yeah… yeah, I do. Not always right that second, because I’m kind of numb and tired, but after, when I’m sitting there with the wrappers or the containers, I feel ashamed. Like… disgusted with myself, honestly.

It’s weird, because at work I’m the guy people count on. I show up, I do what I’m supposed to do, I’ve always thought of myself as pretty disciplined. My dad was big on that too—if you say you’re gonna do something, you do it, no excuses. So then sneaking food around late at night, eating in the car or out in the garage… it makes me feel like I’m letting myself down.
Do you feel like you're eating this extra food because you can't stop yourself, or is it more like you're making a choice to do it?

It feels like I can’t stop, yeah. I mean, I know I’m the one buying it, so it sounds like a choice, but once I start… it’s like a switch flips.

I’ll be standing there thinking, Roy, close the bag, go inside, just be done, and my hands are still reaching in. It’s like when the line at work keeps moving and you just keep doing the next thing without really deciding each time—except this is food, and I hate that I’m doing it.
Do you usually eat this extra food when you're feeling stressed or anxious after work?

I don’t know if I’d call it stressed or anxious exactly. I mean, work can be a lot, sure, but it’s not like I’m sitting there shaking or anything.

Sometimes I’m just worn out, like my brain’s kind of off by the time I clock out. And then there’s the routine of driving past that place, the lights still on, smells coming through the window… Sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess I haven’t really noticed if it’s stress specifically. It’s more like late, tired, and I’m already halfway into it before I think too much.
Do you feel like you're losing control when you're eating this extra food?

Yeah… I mean, that’s probably the best way to put it. Once I start, it feels like the switch is flipped.

I’ll be telling myself, Roy, shut the bag, go inside, you’re done, and then somehow my hand’s still going back in for more. It’s embarrassing to say out loud. It reminds me a little of the line at work when the machine’s running and you just keep feeding parts through without thinking, except… I know that’s not really the same thing. With the food, I’m aware of it, but I’m not stopping.
Do you think you're eating this extra food to try to feel better or improve your mood?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think I’m sitting there thinking, “This will cheer me up,” or anything like that.

It’s more like… I’m tired, and it’s there, and then I’m doing it. Sometimes I guess it feels good for a minute, like when you finally sit down after a long shift and your knees stop aching—well, not exactly that, but you know what I mean. Then pretty quick I’m annoyed with myself.

So… I don’t know if I’d say I’m trying to improve my mood. I haven’t really thought of it that way.
Are you usually hungry when you start eating this extra food after work?

I don’t know that I’ve really paid attention to whether I’m hungry right when it starts.

Sometimes after a shift I could probably eat, sure, but other times it’s more like I just pull in or grab something because it’s on the way. Like, I’ll think about dinner at home, then I’m remembering we’re out of milk or the dog needs food—well, not the dog, we don’t have one now, but you know, errands and stuff—and then I’ve already bought it.

So… I’m not sure. I wouldn’t want to say I’m always hungry, because I honestly don’t know.
Is eating this extra food after work something that happens every time you work a late shift?

Not every single late shift, no. I wish I could say it was that simple, like, “Oh, it only happens on Tuesdays,” or something.

It’s been… the last few months, I’d say usually at least once a week. Sometimes two or three nights, especially if the line’s been a mess or I get out late and I’m already worn down. Some weeks are better, but then it sneaks back in.
Do you think your eating changes when you're feeling emotionally down or upset?

I don’t know. I mean, I get upset like anybody does, but I haven’t really connected it in my head, like “I’m sad, so now I eat more.”

Sometimes if I’ve had a rough day, sure, things kind of slide. But a rough day could be the machine acting up or somebody calling out, or I get home and there’s a bunch of little stuff waiting. My wife used to say I bring work home on my face, which… I guess I do.

So maybe it changes? I’m not sure I’ve noticed it clearly enough to say.
Do you think you would eat this extra food if you weren't driving past the burger place on your way home from work?

I’m not really sure. I mean, that place is right there, you know? You come off the main road and the sign’s lit up, and if traffic’s backed up by the light you’re just sitting there looking at it.

If it wasn’t there… maybe I’d just go home. Or maybe I’d stop somewhere else, I don’t know. There’s a gas station farther down that has those hot food things, though half the time they look like they’ve been sitting there since lunch. I used to stop there more when my schedule was different.

So I guess I can’t say for sure. The burger place definitely makes it easier, but I don’t know if it’s the whole reason.
Do you think you'd still eat this extra food if you found another way to unwind after work?

I’m not sure, honestly. I’d like to think if I had something else to kind of shut my brain off, maybe I’d just go home and do that instead.

But then I think about it and, you know, I’ve tried little things before—not in any organized way, just like telling myself I’ll sit in the garage for a minute or watch something on TV. Half the time I end up messing with something in the house, or my phone rings, or I remember the trash has to go out. It’s funny, when my kids were younger there was always some noise going on, and now even when it’s quiet I don’t always know what to do with myself.

So… maybe another way to unwind would help. I just don’t know if it would stop it all by itself. I haven’t really tested that, I guess.
Do you think you would eat this extra food if you were not alone when you got off work

Yeah… I mean, probably not the same way. If somebody was with me, I’d be more aware of it, I guess.

Like with my wife, I’ll sit down for dinner and kind of act like I’m not that hungry, you know, “oh, I’m fine,” that kind of thing. And then later, if she’s doing laundry or watching one of her shows, I might go out to the truck or find some excuse. It sounds stupid saying it. I just don’t really want her seeing how much I can put away.

It’s not like she’s mean about it. She’s not. She notices things, though. We’ve been married a long time, so she can tell when I’m off. But yeah, if I’m alone after work, it’s easier. If I wasn’t alone, I think I’d hold back more.
Do you feel like you're unable to control how much you eat once you start eating after work?

Yeah… once I start, that’s when it gets away from me.

I’ll be sitting there with the bag or the food, and part of me is saying, Roy, just close it up and go inside. Like, I know what I should do. But my hands just keep going back in. It’s like something flips over, and then I’m not really deciding each bite the way I should be.

And it’s stupid because I can control myself at work fine, you know? I run machines, I check measurements, I don’t just do whatever. But with that food after work, once I’m into it… yeah, it feels like I’m not really in charge of how much anymore.
Do you think you would still eat this extra food if you weren't working the late shifts

I think the late shift has a lot to do with it, yeah. When I get off late, I’m already worn out and I’ll tell myself I’m just stopping for something quick, but then it turns into… two burgers, fries, a shake. And then I still go home and pick through leftovers out in the garage, like I’m having a whole second supper.

If I was working earlier, maybe it wouldn’t line up the same way. I don’t know. I used to work some different hours years back, and traffic was different then too—there was this one place by the plant that closed down, actually—but yeah, the late nights are when it really happens.
Do you think your eating habits would go back to normal if you were to switch to an earlier work shift?

Maybe… but I don’t think it would just magically go back to normal. The late shift is kind of when it happens, you know? I get off and I’m tired, and I’ll stop for takeout thinking it’s just dinner, but then it’s like two burgers, fries, a shake… and then I still go home and end up eating leftovers out in the garage like it’s another whole meal.

I mean, if I got off earlier maybe I wouldn’t hit those same places, or I’d be home with my wife more at a normal dinner time. Back when I worked different hours, the routine was different—though that was years ago, and everything’s changed around the plant since then. But yeah, earlier shift might help. I just don’t know if it would fix it all by itself.
Do you think you eat more when you're feeling upset or emotionally down?

I don’t know… I haven’t really tracked it like that.

I mean, everybody gets upset, right? Some days at the plant are just aggravating, machines acting up, people not doing what they’re supposed to—there was one guy on my line years ago who could make a simple job take twice as long, and it would drive me nuts. But whether that makes me eat more… I’m not sure.

It feels more tied to being tired and getting off late, at least that’s what I notice. I’m not saying emotions have nothing to do with it, I just don’t know that I can point to feeling down and say, yeah, that’s when it happens.
Do you think your eating habits would change if your work schedule changed to only daytime shifts?

I’m not sure. I mean, daytime shifts might help some, just because I wouldn’t be getting off so late and driving past all those places when I’m already wiped out.

But I don’t know if that means my eating would really change, or just change time of day, you know? Sometimes routines stick with you. Like when they switched our break times at the plant, everybody complained for weeks and then somehow people still found a way to do the same stuff, just at different times.

So… maybe it’d be better, but I can’t say for sure.
Do you think your eating would happen if you weren't feeling tired after work?

I’m not really sure. Being tired feels like a big part of it, but I don’t know if taking that away would mean I wouldn’t do it.

Like, some nights I’m just worn out and I don’t feel like thinking, and that’s when it’s easy to pull into a drive-thru. But then there are times on days off where I’m not exactly exhausted, and I still end up wandering into the kitchen too much. So I don’t know how to separate it cleanly.

It’s kind of like at work—everybody blames the night shift for everything, but then you move something to days and some of the same problems follow you. So… maybe it would happen less if I wasn’t tired, but I can’t honestly say it wouldn’t happen.
Do you think your eating behavior after work would be considered a compulsive behavior that you feel you cannot control?

Yeah… I guess “compulsive” is a strong word, but sometimes it does feel like that.

Like once I start, it’s almost like a switch gets flipped. I’ll be sitting there telling myself, Roy, shut the bag and go inside, you don’t need any more, and then my hand’s already reaching back in. It’s stupid, because I know what I’m doing while I’m doing it.

It’s not like at work where if a machine jams, you hit the stop button and fix it. This is more like… I know I should stop, and I mean to stop, but then I just keep going for a while anyway. So yeah, I guess there’s times it feels like I’m not really in control of it.
Do you think you would still eat this extra food if you took a different route home from work that didn't pass by the burger place?

Maybe not that exact burger place, but… yeah, I think I’d still probably find something.

I mean, the burger place is convenient, sure. It’s right there, and after a late shift it’s easy to just pull in. But the part that worries me is, even when I tell myself I’m only grabbing something quick, I’ll end up getting two burgers, fries, a shake… and then I still go home and start picking through leftovers out in the garage like I’m having a whole second supper.

So taking a different road might slow me down a little, I guess. But I don’t think the road is the whole problem. It’s more like once I’m in that after-work mode, I’m looking for food one way or another.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is a coping mechanism for emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you think you eat more when you're feeling upset or emotionally down?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether emotional distress or feeling down triggers increased eating. The provided symptom profile includes negative feelings after binge episodes, but not eating more because of feeling upset beforehand.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… I haven’t really tracked it like that.

I mean, everybody gets upset, right? Some days at the plant are just aggravating, machines acting up, people not doing what they’re supposed to—there was one guy on my line years ago who could make a simple job take twice as long, and it would drive me nuts. But whether that makes me eat more… I’m not sure.

It feels more tied to being tired and getting off late, at least that’s what I notice. I’m not saying emotions have nothing to do with it, I just don’t know that I can point to feeling down and say, yeah, that’s when it happens.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is a habitual response to working late shifts
doctor.question: Do you think your eating habits would change if your work schedule changed to only daytime shifts?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether changing to daytime shifts would change the eating habits, which is about a potential schedule-related trigger or cause. The provided symptom profile does not include an item specifically covering work schedule effects or triggers.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, daytime shifts might help some, just because I wouldn’t be getting off so late and driving past all those places when I’m already wiped out.

But I don’t know if that means my eating would really change, or just change time of day, you know? Sometimes routines stick with you. Like when they switched our break times at the plant, everybody complained for weeks and then somehow people still found a way to do the same stuff, just at different times.

So… maybe it’d be better, but I can’t say for sure.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating habits are related to emotional states
doctor.question: Do you think your eating would happen if you weren't feeling tired after work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about tiredness after work as a possible trigger or condition for the eating, but the symptom profile does not include a specific item about fatigue-related triggers.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. Being tired feels like a big part of it, but I don’t know if taking that away would mean I wouldn’t do it.

Like, some nights I’m just worn out and I don’t feel like thinking, and that’s when it’s easy to pull into a drive-thru. But then there are times on days off where I’m not exactly exhausted, and I still end up wandering into the kitchen too much. So I don’t know how to separate it cleanly.

It’s kind of like at work—everybody blames the night shift for everything, but then you move something to days and some of the same problems follow you. So… maybe it would happen less if I wasn’t tired, but I can’t honestly say it wouldn’t happen.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is a result of an emotional eating disorder or a disorder related to other factors such as stress or habit
doctor.question: Do you think your eating behavior after work would be considered a compulsive behavior that you feel you cannot control?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start, it feels like the switch is flipped and even while I’m telling myself, 'Roy, shut the bag and go inside,' my hands just keep reaching for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the eating feels compulsive and uncontrollable, which directly matches loss of control during binge episodes.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I guess “compulsive” is a strong word, but sometimes it does feel like that.

Like once I start, it’s almost like a switch gets flipped. I’ll be sitting there telling myself, Roy, shut the bag and go inside, you don’t need any more, and then my hand’s already reaching back in. It’s stupid, because I know what I’m doing while I’m doing it.

It’s not like at work where if a machine jams, you hit the stop button and fix it. This is more like… I know I should stop, and I mean to stop, but then I just keep going for a while anyway. So yeah, I guess there’s times it feels like I’m not really in control of it.

patient.answer:
Maybe not that exact burger place, but… yeah, I think I’d still probably find something.

I mean, the burger place is convenient, sure. It’s right there, and after a late shift it’s easy to just pull in. But the part that worries me is, even when I tell myself I’m only grabbing something quick, I’ll end up getting two burgers, fries, a shake… and then I still go home and start picking through leftovers out in the garage like I’m having a whole second supper.

So taking a different road might slow me down a little, I guess. But I don’t think the road is the whole problem. It’s more like once I’m in that after-work mode, I’m looking for food one way or another.
